# Text tools and pipes {#sec-text-tools}

**Core.** Work through it, with the exercises.

::: {.callout-note .goals icon=false}
## Learning goals

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

1. Connect commands with pipes, and send output to a file with `>`,
   `>>`, and `tee`, without overwriting an input.
2. Keep results (standard output) and messages (standard error) apart,
   and capture or discard each on purpose.
3. Count, sort, and summarise columns with `cut`, `sort`, `uniq -c`,
   and `wc`, and find lines with `grep`.
4. Write a basic regular expression and use it in `grep` and `sed`, and
   select and compute on fields with `awk`.
5. Read and write gzipped files through a pipe, and say when a
   format-aware tool is safer than a text tool.
:::

## What this chapter does {#sec-text-tools-intro}

Most bioinformatics files are plain text with one record per line:
sample sheets, annotation (GTF), tables of counts. FASTQ is text too,
with one read per four lines in the book's files. So a dozen small tools,
each doing one job, answer most quick questions about these files when
you join them with `|`: how many reads, how long, how many of each kind,
which lines match. That is the whole "Unix philosophy" this chapter
needs: small tools, joined together.

You have run pipes already. In @sec-orientation you typed
`gunzip -c … | wc -l` and wrote a result with `>`; @sec-organizing-projects's
script ends in `2>&1 | tee "$log"`; @sec-shell-basics used
`history | tail`. This chapter explains each piece, so you can change
those commands and write your own.

Commands run on your laptop, from the project folder. You only **read**
the project's files here. Everything you write goes to a scratch folder,
`~/bioinf-computing-ch06`, never into `data/`; the one exception is your
notes in `NOTEBOOK.md`, as in earlier chapters. Make the scratch folder
and go to the project:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch06
cd ~/bioinf-computing
```

Stay in `~/bioinf-computing` for the whole chapter: `pixi run` finds the
book's environment from there, and the commands use paths such as
`data/raw/…` that start from it. Every file the chapter writes is named
with its full scratch path, `~/bioinf-computing-ch06/…`.

The outputs shown were captured with GNU grep 3.12, GNU sed 4.10, GNU
Awk 5.4.1, GNU coreutils 9.11, GNU gzip 1.15, and seqkit 2.14.0, in the
`en_US.UTF-8` locale. Other versions give the same results except where
a block says otherwise.

## Pipes {#sec-text-tools-pipes}

Rerun two commands from @sec-orientation, this time on the project's
copy of the file:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | head -n 8
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | wc -l
```

```{.console}
@SRR6357070.25017281 25017281/1 kraken:taxid|4932
CCTGAATCGAGAAGGAGGTGTCCAGGGAGTTCATCATCAGAATGATTAGTATGATTTACTGTAGATTCAGTAAGTTTCTGGCCTAAGATGAAGGTCGTGCT
+
BBBBBFFFFFFFBFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFBFFFBFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFBFFBFFFFFFF
@SRR6357070.6710070 6710070/1 kraken:taxid|4932
GTCAGATTGGAAGTCATGGTCAGATTCTATGTTAAGATCATCGGATTGTTGGATCTCATTTGACGCAATGAACGATTGATATGAAGCAGTTAAACGGTTTA
+
BBBBBFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFB
200000
```

**Take the pipe apart.** `gunzip -c` on its own decompresses the file
and prints all 200,000 lines to the screen: do not run it alone, or you
will watch reads scroll past for a while (stop it with
{{< kbd Ctrl-C >}}). `head -n 8` on its own, with no file name, waits
for you to type lines; press {{< kbd Ctrl-C >}} to get the prompt back
(stopping programs properly is @sec-linux-system). Joined by `|`, the
first program's output becomes the second one's input, and you see only
what you asked for.

**Now name it.** Every program has one **standard input** (stdin) and
one **standard output** (stdout). By default stdin is your keyboard and
stdout is your screen. The pipe `|` connects the stdout of the program
on its left to the stdin of the program on its right. No file is written
in between, and both programs run at the same time: `head` starts
printing while `gunzip` is still working.

A pipe saves you an intermediate **file**, not all memory or disk use.
`sort`, for example, must read all its input before it can print the
first line, and for big inputs it writes temporary files of its own
(where, on a cluster, is @sec-hpc-slurm).

Programs that read stdin when you give them no file name are called
**filters**: `head`, `wc`, `sort`, `cut`, `grep`, `sed`, `awk`, and
`gzip` all are. That is what `[FILE]...` meant in the usage line of
`gzip` in @sec-getting-help: with no file, it reads stdin.

**Build a pipeline one step at a time.** Ask a real question: how long
are the reads? Start with the sequence lines, which in this file are line
2 of every 4, and look at the result before adding the next step:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2' | head -n 3
```

```{.console}
CCTGAATCGAGAAGGAGGTGTCCAGGGAGTTCATCATCAGAATGATTAGTATGATTTACTGTAGATTCAGTAAGTTTCTGGCCTAAGATGAAGGTCGTGCT
GTCAGATTGGAAGTCATGGTCAGATTCTATGTTAAGATCATCGGATTGTTGGATCTCATTTGACGCAATGAACGATTGATATGAAGCAGTTAAACGGTTTA
GGAATAGTATATGTTGAGCAAGTGTGTTGATGTAGTATAGTAAGTCAAATCTAAATTTATATCCAACATATGAAGCTAGACCAATCAACTTTTGCATTTCA
```

Sequences only. Now print each length, sort the lengths, and count each
value:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz \
  | awk 'NR % 4 == 2 {print length($0)}' \
  | sort \
  | uniq -c
```

```{.console}
  50000 101
```

Every one of the 50,000 reads is 101 bases long. A long pipeline can be
broken over lines with `\` at the end of each line, one step per line,
as here; it is still one command. @fig-pipeline-steps shows what each
step passes on, on a toy file of three reads.

::: {#fig-pipeline-steps}
{{< svg ../figures/pipeline-steps.svg >}}

The read-length pipeline on a toy file of three reads, one program at a
time. Each step prints lines that the next step reads; no file is
written in between. (In the chapter's command the two `awk` steps are
one `awk`.) Use *Next* to step through.
:::

`awk 'NR % 4 == 2'` means "print line 2, 6, 10, …": `NR` is the line
number and `%` the remainder after division. @sec-text-tools-sed-awk
explains `awk`. For now, note the assumption: this works **because this
file has exactly four lines per read**, as you checked in
@sec-orientation. FASTQ in general does not promise that
(@sec-fasta-fastq), which is why format-aware tools exist
(@sec-text-tools-format-aware).

Two more things are worth knowing now. First, `head` stops reading after
8 lines, so `gunzip` is stopped too, before it reaches the end of the
file. That is normal. Bash records each program's exit status in the
array `PIPESTATUS`:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | head -n 8 > /dev/null
echo "${PIPESTATUS[@]}"
```

```{.console}
141 0
```

`141` means `gunzip` was stopped because nobody was reading any more;
`0` is `head`'s success. (`> /dev/null` throws the output away;
@sec-text-tools-streams.) The exact number can vary with the program and
the timing. It matters in scripts that stop on any error
(`set -o pipefail`, @sec-shell-scripts). Second, because it stops early,
`gunzip -c … | head` says nothing about whether the **rest** of the file
is intact. Checking the whole file is `gzip -t`, from @sec-orientation.

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
A pipe `|` joins one program's standard output to the next program's
standard input. Build pipelines one step at a time, and look at the
output after each step before adding the next.
:::

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** What does
`gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | head -n 4 | wc -l` print?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
`4`. `wc` counts only the four lines `head` passed on; it never sees the
rest of the file.
:::
:::

## Redirection and the `>` trap {#sec-text-tools-redirection}

@sec-orientation saved a read count with `>` and added the second file's
count with `>>`. Do the same into the scratch folder, running the `>`
line **twice**:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
echo "SRR6357070_1 reads: $(( $(gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | wc -l) / 4 ))" > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/fastq_summary.txt
echo "SRR6357070_1 reads: $(( $(gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | wc -l) / 4 ))" > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/fastq_summary.txt
cat ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/fastq_summary.txt
```

```{.console}
SRR6357070_1 reads: 50000
```

One line: the second `>` replaced the first. Now the R2 line, with
`>>`, also twice:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
echo "SRR6357070_2 reads: $(( $(gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz | wc -l) / 4 ))" >> ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/fastq_summary.txt
echo "SRR6357070_2 reads: $(( $(gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz | wc -l) / 4 ))" >> ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/fastq_summary.txt
cat ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/fastq_summary.txt
```

```{.console}
SRR6357070_1 reads: 50000
SRR6357070_2 reads: 50000
SRR6357070_2 reads: 50000
```

`>>` adds to the end every time, so the R2 line is there twice. Rerunning
a command that appends is a common way to get duplicated rows. `>`
**replaces** a file's contents; `>>` **appends**. Both create the file if
it does not exist.

`<` goes the other way: it connects a file to a program's stdin.

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
wc -l ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/fastq_summary.txt
wc -l < ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/fastq_summary.txt
```

```{.console}
3 /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch06/fastq_summary.txt
3
```

Given a file name, `wc` prints the name too; reading stdin, it has no
name to print. That makes `<` handy when you want only the number.

### The trap: `cmd file > file`

Make a three-line toy file and try to sort it "in place":

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
printf 'b\na\nc\n' > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.txt
cat ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.txt
sort ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.txt > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.txt
wc -c ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.txt
```

```{.console}
b
a
c
0 /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.txt
```

Zero bytes: the file is empty, with no error and no warning. The reason
is the order of events (@fig-overwrite). Bash sets up the redirection
**before** it starts the program, and setting up `>` opens the file for
writing, which empties it. Only then does `sort` start, read the now
empty `toy.txt`, and write nothing. The same happens with `grep`, `cut`,
`awk`, and any other command whose input and `>` output are the same
file.

::: {#fig-overwrite}
{{< svg ../figures/overwrite.svg >}}

Why `sort toy.txt > toy.txt` leaves an empty file. The shell empties
`toy.txt` before `sort` starts, so `sort` reads nothing. The safe route:
write a new file, check it, then `mv` it over the old one.
:::

The fix is the route in the figure: write to a **new** name, check it,
then move it into place.

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
printf 'b\na\nc\n' > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.txt
sort ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.txt > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.sorted.txt
cat ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.sorted.txt
mv ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.sorted.txt ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.txt
```

```{.console}
a
b
c
```

This is exactly what @sec-organizing-projects's script does: `seqkit`
writes `results/read_counts.tsv.tmp`, and only after that succeeds does
`mv` put it in place of `read_counts.tsv`. Now you can see why.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: `cmd file > file` empties the file
The shell empties the output file before the command reads it. Write to
a new name, check the result, then `mv` it over the original.
:::

::: {.callout-caution .misconception}
## Misconception: "`sort data.txt > data.txt` sorts the file in place"
**Reality.** The shell empties `data.txt` before `sort` starts, so you
are left with an empty file. Redirection never edits a file in place.
:::

**A safety net: `noclobber`.** @sec-shell-basics showed `cp -n`, which
refuses to overwrite. Bash has the same idea for `>`. Try it inside
`( … )`, which runs the commands in a separate copy of the shell, so the
setting goes away afterwards:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
( set -o noclobber; echo x > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.txt )
echo $?
```

```{.console}
bash: /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.txt: cannot overwrite existing file
1
```

With `noclobber` on, `>` refuses to replace an existing file, and `>|`
forces it. It guards `>` only: `>>`, `tee`, `cp`, `mv`, and `sed -i` still
overwrite. You could turn it on for good in your `~/.bashrc`
(@sec-linux-system), but this book does not, because later chapters
overwrite files on purpose. The habits that protect you are the
`.tmp`-then-`mv` route and @sec-organizing-projects's read-only
`data/raw/`:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
echo test > data/raw/notes.txt
```

```{.console}
bash: data/raw/notes.txt: Permission denied
```

The same message stops `sort data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz >
data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz` before it can empty the file. (What
permissions are is @sec-linux-system.) Note the two quieter dangers of
`>`: on a mistyped name it silently makes a new file, and on the right
name it silently replaces the old contents.

### `tee`: save and see

Sometimes you want a result in a file **and** on the screen. `tee`
copies its stdin to a file and to its stdout:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
pixi run seqkit stats -T \
  data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz \
  data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz \
  | tee ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts.tsv \
  | cut -f1,4
```

```{.console}
file	num_seqs
data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz	50000
data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz	50000
```

The full eight-column table went into `counts.tsv`, and the screen shows
only columns 1 and 4 (`cut`, @sec-text-tools-counting). `-T` makes seqkit
print a tab-separated table, which `cut` needs; seqkit's default table is
laid out for people to read. You will also see a `processed files` line,
which the next section explains. `tee -a` appends instead of replacing;
@sec-organizing-projects's script used `tee "$log"` to save its messages
while showing them.

: Redirection operators. `cmd` is any command. {#tbl-redirection}

| Operator | What it does | Example | Danger |
|:---------|:-------------|:--------|:-------|
| `\|` | stdout of the left command to stdin of the right | `gunzip -c f.gz \| wc -l` | the left command's errors still reach the screen |
| `>` | stdout to a file, replacing it | `cmd > out.txt` | empties the file first, even if it is the input |
| `>>` | stdout to the end of a file | `cmd >> log.txt` | rerunning duplicates lines |
| `<` | a file to stdin | `wc -l < f.txt` | |
| `2>` | stderr to a file | `cmd 2> err.txt` | |
| `2>&1` | stderr to wherever stdout goes now | `cmd > all.txt 2>&1` | order matters (@sec-text-tools-streams) |
| `&>` | both streams to a file (bash) | `cmd &> all.txt` | results and messages mixed |
| `>\|` | `>` even when `noclobber` is on | `cmd >\| out.txt` | |
| `tee f` | stdin to a file and to stdout | `cmd \| tee out.txt` | replaces `f`; `tee -a` appends |
| `/dev/null` | a file that discards everything | `cmd 2> /dev/null` | hides messages you may need |

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** You run `grep -v '^#' notes.txt > notes.txt`. What
is in `notes.txt` now?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Nothing. The shell emptied `notes.txt` before `grep` started, so `grep`
read an empty file. Write to `notes.clean.txt`, check it, then `mv`.
:::
:::

## Standard output and standard error {#sec-text-tools-streams}

Send the seqkit table into a file:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
pixi run seqkit stats -T data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz \
  data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts.tsv
```

```{.console}
processed files:  2 / 2 [======] ETA: 0s. done
```

The table went into `counts.tsv`, but a line still appeared on the
screen. If `>` sends "the output" to a file, where did this line come
from?

**Two output streams.** Every program has a second output,
**standard error** (stderr). By convention, programs write their
**results** to stdout and their **messages**, progress, warnings, and
errors to stderr. Both go to your terminal by default, so they look the
same until you redirect one of them (@fig-streams). `>` and `|` carry
stdout only; stderr still reaches the screen. seqkit's progress line is
on stderr, which is why it stayed. (On screen it updates itself in
place; saved to a file, it shows the cursor codes it uses for that.
@sec-organizing-projects's script runs `seqkit stats --quiet`, which
turns the line off.)

::: {#fig-streams}
{{< svg ../figures/streams.svg >}}

A program has one input (stdin) and two outputs: stdout for results and
stderr for messages. By default both reach the terminal. `> file` moves
only stdout; a pipe carries only stdout, so the error from `gunzip`
skips `wc` and goes straight to the screen.
:::

To send stderr somewhere, put its number in front of `>`. Stdin is
stream 0, stdout 1, and stderr 2, so `2>` redirects stderr. Go back to
@sec-getting-help's truncated file. Make a copy in the scratch folder
and run seqkit on it, with each stream to its own file:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
head -c 1000000 data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/broken.fastq.gz
pixi run seqkit stats -T ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/broken.fastq.gz \
  > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/out.tsv \
  2> ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/err.txt
cat ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/out.tsv
cat ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/err.txt
```

```{.console}
file	format	type	num_seqs	sum_len	min_len	avg_len	max_len
[ERRO] /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch06/broken.fastq.gz: unexpected EOF
[ERRO]
```

The header row (a result) is in `out.tsv`; the error is in `err.txt`.
Nothing reached the screen. `cat` shows `[ERRO]` in red, as seqkit
printed it. `cat -A`, which shows every invisible character, reveals how:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cat -A ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/err.txt
```

```{.console}
^[[31m[ERRO]^[[0m /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch06/broken.fastq.gz: unexpected EOF$
^[[31m[ERRO]^[[0m $
```

`^[[31m` and `^[[0m` are colour codes: "red on", "colour off". `$` marks
each line's end. Colour codes end up in log files this way; they are
harmless, but they are why a log can look odd in an editor. (`cat -A`
returns in @sec-text-tools-counting for tabs, and @sec-linux-system uses
it for Windows line endings.)

**Both streams into one file.** `2>&1` means "send stderr to wherever
stdout is going **now**". So the order matters:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
pixi run seqkit stats -T ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/broken.fastq.gz \
  > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/both.txt 2>&1
```

puts both streams in `both.txt`. Written the other way round,
`2>&1 > both.txt`, stderr is pointed at the screen (where stdout was at
that moment) and only stdout goes to the file. Bash's shorthand `&>`
does the first version. Use these for **logs**, never for results: a
results table with error lines in it breaks the next tool that reads it.
@sec-organizing-projects's script wrapped its commands in `{ … }`, then
sent `2>&1 | tee "$log"`, so its log keeps the messages from both
streams, while the results went to their own file with `>`.

`/dev/null` is a special file that discards whatever is written to it.
`2> /dev/null` hides messages. Use it only for messages you have read
and know you do not need, such as seqkit's progress line; never to make
a screen of errors look clean.

**The pipe carries stdout only.** Count the lines of the broken file:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/broken.fastq.gz | wc -l
echo $?
```

```{.console}

gzip: /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch06/broken.fastq.gz: unexpected end of file
89515
0
```

Read this carefully. Decompression failed partway, after producing some
text. The error went to stderr, around the pipe, to your screen. `wc`
successfully counted the text it received: 89,515 lines. That count is
**incomplete** and cannot be used as a read count. And `echo $?` says
`0`, because a pipeline's exit status is the status of its **last**
command, `wc`, which did its job. `"${PIPESTATUS[@]}"` here would show
`1 0`: `gunzip` failed, `wc` succeeded. (The exact count depends on the
gzip version: Apple's gzip on a Mac stopped at 89,253. Either way, it is
partial.)

Do not try to spot damage by checking whether a line count divides by
4: another cut could land on a multiple of 4 and still be wrong. Know
your expected count (50,000 reads here), and read the messages.
`set -o pipefail` (@sec-shell-scripts) makes a pipeline fail when any
stage reports failure, but it cannot help when a tool reports success
despite an error, as seqkit 2.14.0 did in @sec-getting-help. That is why
the result checks from @sec-getting-help still matter.

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
By convention, results go to stdout and messages to stderr. `>` and `|`
carry only stdout, so errors still reach the screen, and a pipeline can
"succeed" on broken input. This is a convention tools follow, not a
rule the shell enforces: some tools mix the two or write their own log
files.
:::

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** A command prints a table and some warnings. You want
the table in `out.tsv` and the warnings in `run.log`. Write the
redirection. And after `seqkit stats … > counts.tsv`, why was a
progress line still on the screen?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
`cmd > out.tsv 2> run.log`. The progress line is on stderr, and `>`
redirects only stdout.
:::
:::

## Counting and summarising: `wc`, `cut`, `sort`, `uniq` {#sec-text-tools-counting}

Start with a table small enough to check by eye: the practice sample
table from @sec-shell-basics. If you built Chapter 5's practice folder,
it is `~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/meta/samples.tsv`. Either way, make
the chapter's own copy with this block (the same lines Chapter 5 used;
the list and `printf` are explained in @sec-shell-scripts):

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
rows=(sample run_folder condition reads
  sample_C "Run 3 final" treated 12
  sample_A run1 control 9
  sample_B run2 control 30
  sample_E run5 treated 105
  sample_B run2 control 30
  sample_D run4 control 8)
printf '%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n' "${rows[@]}" > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv
md5sum ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv
```

```{.console}
971d8f742cb76a8d181d3bdc3dcbceaa  /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv
```

If you have Chapter 5's file, `md5sum` on it gives the same checksum.
From here on the chapter uses the copy in `~/bioinf-computing-ch06`. (It
is not the project's `data/meta/samples.tsv`, which has different
columns.) Look at it:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cat ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv
wc -l ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv
cat -A ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv | head -n 3
```

```{.console}
sample	run_folder	condition	reads
sample_C	Run 3 final	treated	12
sample_A	run1	control	9
sample_B	run2	control	30
sample_E	run5	treated	105
sample_B	run2	control	30
sample_D	run4	control	8
7 /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv
sample^Irun_folder^Icondition^Ireads$
sample_C^IRun 3 final^Itreated^I12$
sample_A^Irun1^Icontrol^I9$
```

A header and six rows, separated by tabs (`cat -A` shows each tab as
`^I`). By eye: `sample_B` is listed twice, on rows 3 and 5. Can the
tools find that?

**`uniq` only merges neighbours.** `cut -f1` takes column 1; `uniq -c`
counts repeated lines:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cut -f1 ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv | uniq -c
```

```{.console}
      1 sample
      1 sample_C
      1 sample_A
      1 sample_B
      1 sample_E
      1 sample_B
      1 sample_D
```

`sample_B` appears twice, each with count 1. `uniq` compares each line
only with the line before it, and the two `sample_B` lines are not next
to each other. Sort first, so equal values become neighbours:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cut -f1 ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv | sort | uniq -c
cut -f1 ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv | sort | uniq -d
```

```{.console}
      1 sample
      1 sample_A
      2 sample_B
      1 sample_C
      1 sample_D
      1 sample_E
sample_B
```

`2 sample_B`. `uniq -d` prints only the lines that occur more than once.
**`sort | uniq -c`** is the habit: it counts equal values wherever they
sit in the file.

::: {.callout-caution .misconception}
## Misconception: "`uniq` removes or counts all duplicate lines"
**Reality.** `uniq` only merges identical lines that are next to each
other. Sort first: `sort | uniq -c`.
:::

**Skip the header.** Count the conditions:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cut -f3 ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv | sort | uniq -c
tail -n +2 ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv | cut -f3 | sort | uniq -c
```

```{.console}
      1 condition
      4 control
      2 treated
      4 control
      2 treated
```

The first version counted the header as a value. `tail -n +2` prints
from line 2 onwards, which drops it. (`tail -n 2`, without the `+`, would
print the last two lines.)

**Numbers sort as text.** Sort the rows by the `reads` column, as text
and then as numbers:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
tail -n +2 ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv | sort -t$'\t' -k4,4
tail -n +2 ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv | sort -t$'\t' -k4,4n
```

```{.console}
sample_E	run5	treated	105
sample_C	Run 3 final	treated	12
sample_B	run2	control	30
sample_B	run2	control	30
sample_D	run4	control	8
sample_A	run1	control	9
sample_D	run4	control	8
sample_A	run1	control	9
sample_C	Run 3 final	treated	12
sample_B	run2	control	30
sample_B	run2	control	30
sample_E	run5	treated	105
```

As text, `105` comes first, because `sort` compares character by
character and `1` comes before `3`, `8`, and `9`. With `n`, the column is
compared as numbers: 8, 9, 12, 30, 30, 105. The pieces: `-t$'\t'` says
the fields are separated by tabs (`$'\t'` is how you type a tab
character in bash); `-k4,4` sorts on field 4 only, from field 4 to field
4; the `n` after it makes that key numeric.

**The duplicate matters.** `sort -u` keeps one copy of each identical
line:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
tail -n +2 ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv | sort -u
```

```{.console}
sample_A	run1	control	9
sample_B	run2	control	30
sample_C	Run 3 final	treated	12
sample_D	run4	control	8
sample_E	run5	treated	105
```

Five samples. The header was removed with `tail -n +2` **before**
sorting, so it cannot end up among the data. The `reads` column adds up
to 194 with the duplicate and 164 without it (you will compute both with
`awk` in @sec-text-tools-sed-awk): a duplicated metadata row inflates
totals silently. `sort -u` removes only rows that are identical in
every column. Two rows with the same sample name and **different**
values are a conflict to resolve, not a duplicate to drop
(@sec-tabular-data). Note also that `sample_D` and `sample_E` have no read
files in Chapter 5's practice folder: a sample table and the files on
disk can disagree, which @sec-tabular-data checks properly.

### The real sample sheet

@sec-organizing-projects saved nf-core's sample sheet unchanged as
`data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv`. It is comma-separated, so tell `cut`
the delimiter with `-d,`:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cut -d, -f1 data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv | sort | uniq -c
```

```{.console}
      1 RAP1_IAA_30M_REP1
      1 RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP1
      2 RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP2
      1 sample
      2 WT_REP1
      1 WT_REP2
```

Seven runs under five test labels: `WT_REP1` and
`RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP2` each group two runs, so the test exercises merging
(they are not one sample sequenced twice;
@sec-organizing-projects-metadata checked them against the archive). The
header `sample` is counted too; `tail -n +2` removes it. Here the
repeated labels already sit next to each other in the file, so
`uniq -c` alone would happen to give the same counts. The practice table
is why you sort anyway. One more column, the strandedness setting:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
tail -n +2 data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv | cut -d, -f4 | sort | uniq -c
```

```{.console}
      2 auto
      5 reverse
```

**Sort order depends on the locale.** Look again at where `sample` landed
above: between the `RAP1_…` and `WT_…` names. Now sort with
`LC_ALL=C`:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cut -d, -f1 data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv | LC_ALL=C sort | uniq -c
```

```{.console}
      1 RAP1_IAA_30M_REP1
      1 RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP1
      2 RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP2
      2 WT_REP1
      1 WT_REP2
      1 sample
```

Same counts, different order. Your **locale** (language settings) tells
`sort` how to order letters. In `en_US.UTF-8`, upper and lower case are
mixed together, as in a dictionary. In the `C` locale, characters are
ordered by their byte values, so all capitals come before all lower-case
letters. `LC_ALL=C` in front of a command sets it for that command only.
Use it when the order must be the same on every computer. Tools that
compare sorted files, such as `join` and `comm`, need their input sorted
by the same rules they use themselves; if you sort with `LC_ALL=C`, run
them with `LC_ALL=C` too. Which locale you have by default depends on the system: WSL's
Ubuntu uses `C.UTF-8`, which already sorts like `C`, so there both
commands give this second order. Your settings are @sec-linux-system.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Sort before you count
Sort before `uniq -c`, so equal values are counted wherever they are in
the file. Use `LC_ALL=C sort` when the order must be reproducible.
:::

### The annotation

Now the yeast annotation, `data/ref/genes.gtf.gz`, read through the
`data/ref` link. A GTF file has nine tab-separated columns, and column 3
is the feature type. Count the types, most common first:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c data/ref/genes.gtf.gz | cut -f3 | sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr
```

```{.console}
    129 exon
    124 transcript
    118 CDS
    115 start_codon
    114 stop_codon
```

The final `sort -k1,1nr`, piece by piece: sort on field 1 (the counts),
as numbers (`n`), in reverse (`r`), largest first. With no `-t`, `sort`
splits fields at blanks, and the leading spaces from `uniq -c` are
skipped. What is **missing** is a finding too: there are no `gene`
lines. Many GTF files have one per gene; this test file has transcripts,
exons, coding parts (CDS), and start and stop codons only, 600 lines in
all. A tool that expects `gene` lines would find none here.

Now column 1, the sequence (chromosome) names:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c data/ref/genes.gtf.gz | cut -f1 | sort | uniq -c
gunzip -c data/ref/genome.fa.gz | grep '^>'
```

```{.console}
    599 I
      1 not_in_genome
```

```{.console}
>I
```

You may remember the `not_in_genome` line from Exercise 5 of
@sec-shell-basics, where it was the first line of the file. Counting
shows that it is the only one: 599 lines are on chromosome `I`, the one
sequence in the genome (the `grep` prints FASTA header lines, which start
with `>`; @sec-text-tools-grep). nf-core put that line there on purpose,
to test that the pipeline copes with an annotation line on a sequence the
genome does not have ([nf-core/test-datasets commit
`1b17b24`](https://github.com/nf-core/test-datasets/commit/1b17b24),
"Add gtf line using chromosome not in genome"). Real annotations and
genomes do not always match either (@sec-fasta-fastq). Two minutes of
counting found something you would otherwise meet as a pipeline error.

**Text sort vs numeric sort, on real coordinates.** Column 4 holds start
positions. Take the first 12 transcript starts and sort them both ways:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c data/ref/genes.gtf.gz | grep -w transcript | cut -f4 | head -n 12 \
  > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/starts.txt
sort ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/starts.txt | tr '\n' ' '; echo
sort -n ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/starts.txt | tr '\n' ' '; echo
```

```{.console}
10091 11565 12046 13363 1807 21566 22395 24000 2480 335 538 7235
335 538 1807 2480 7235 10091 11565 12046 13363 21566 22395 24000
```

Text order puts `10091` before `1807` and `335` near the end. (`tr '\n' '
'` turns newlines into spaces, so the list fits on one line; `echo` ends
the line.) Sorting coordinates as text is a classic way to break
interval files (@sec-intervals-variants).

::: {.callout-caution .misconception}
## Misconception: "`sort` puts numbers in numeric order"
**Reality.** By default `sort` compares text, character by character, so
`10091` comes before `1807`. Use `sort -n`, with `-k` to choose the
column.
:::

**One more count, on the reads.** How many distinct sequences are there
among R1's 50,000 reads, and which is most common?

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2' | sort -u | wc -l
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2' \
  | sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr | head -n 3 | cut -c1-40
```

```{.console}
21662
    208 GTTAGGAGTGTGCAATACCTTTATTGATGTTT
    186 CTTTGACCCAGGTAGGTAGGAATTGAGAGGGA
    123 CTTTAAATGGGTCAGGGAATTCGGTAGGAGAT
```

21,662 distinct sequences; the most common one appears 208 times.
(`cut -c1-40` keeps the first 40 characters of each line, to fit.) What
duplicated reads mean for an RNA-seq experiment is a quality-control
question for the Genomics and Transcriptomics books; here, the point is
that the same `sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr` pattern answered it.

: The counting tools used in this chapter. {#tbl-text-tools}

| Tool | What it does | Flags used here | Example |
|:-----|:-------------|:----------------|:--------|
| `wc` | counts lines, words, bytes | `-l` lines, `-c` bytes | `wc -l samples.tsv` |
| `cut` | keeps columns (fields) or characters | `-f` fields, `-d` delimiter (tab by default), `-c` characters | `cut -d, -f1 sheet.csv` |
| `sort` | sorts lines | `-n` numeric, `-k2,2` key, `-t` separator, `-r` reverse, `-u` unique | `sort -t$'\t' -k4,4n` |
| `uniq` | merges identical **neighbouring** lines | `-c` count, `-d` only repeated | `sort \| uniq -c` |
| `head`, `tail` | first or last lines | `-n 5`; `tail -n +2` from line 2 | `tail -n +2 samples.tsv` |
| `tr` | replaces characters | `tr '\n' ' '` | newlines to spaces |
| `paste` | joins lines side by side | `paste - - - -` four lines into one | (reference) |
| `column -t` | lines up columns for reading | `column -t -s$'\t'` | (reference) |

`cut` splits on tabs by default, which is why tab-separated files are
easy to work with. A comma-separated file with commas **inside** quoted
fields (`"Smith, J"`) defeats `cut -d,`; that needs a real table reader
(@sec-tabular-data).

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** `cut -d, -f1 samplesheet_upstream.csv | uniq -c`
gives the right counts, but `cut -f1 samples.tsv | uniq -c` on the
practice table does not. Why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
In the sample sheet the repeated labels are on neighbouring lines; in the
practice table the two `sample_B` rows are not, and `uniq` only merges
neighbours. Sort first.
:::
:::

## Finding lines: `grep` {#sec-text-tools-grep}

`grep` prints the lines that match a pattern. With `-c` it counts them.
Count the read headers in both mate files:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | grep -c '^@SRR'
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz | grep -c '^@SRR'
```

```{.console}
50000
50000
```

`^` means "at the start of the line" (@sec-text-tools-regex). Now a real
question from @sec-getting-help: the paper's methods trimmed the adapter
`AGATCGGAAGAGC` with cutadapt. How many reads contain that exact
sequence? Search the sequence lines only:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2' | grep -c AGATCGGAAGAGC
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2' | grep -c AGATCGGAAGAGC
```

```{.console}
1916
1910
```

1,916 reads in R1 and 1,910 in R2 contain this **exact** 13-letter
motif. That is not a measure of adapter contamination: partial adapters
at a read's end and adapters with a sequencing error are missed. Trimming
tools and quality reports measure that properly (the applied books).
Note what `-c` counts: matching **lines**. A line with the motif twice
counts once; `grep -o` prints each match on its own line, if you want to
count occurrences.

A gene in the annotation:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c data/ref/genes.gtf.gz | grep -w 'gene_name "CDC19"' | cut -f1-8
```

```{.console}
I	ensembl	CDS	71786	73285	.	+	0
I	ensembl	exon	71786	73288	.	+	.
I	ensembl	start_codon	71786	71788	.	+	0
I	ensembl	transcript	71786	73288	.	+	.
I	ensembl	stop_codon	73286	73288	.	+	0
```

Five lines for CDC19 (pyruvate kinase), on the `+` strand from 71,786
to 73,288. `-w` matches whole words only, so a search for `CDC1` would
not match `CDC19`. The pattern is in single quotes because it contains
spaces and double quotes (@sec-shell-basics).

### The `@` trap

Would `grep -c '^@'` also count the reads? On this file, yes:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | grep -c '^@'
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 0' | grep -o . | sort | uniq -c
```

```{.console}
50000
 216720 /
    280 #
 191521 <
  11539 7
 486514 B
4143426 F
```

The second command lists every character used in the quality lines
(line 4 of every 4; `grep -o .` prints each character on its own line).
This file uses only six quality characters, and `@` is not one of them.
But `@` **is** a valid quality character (a base quality of 31,
@sec-fasta-fastq), so in other files a quality line can start with `@`.
Here is a two-read toy file where one does:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
printf '@r1\nACGT\n+\n@III\n@r2\nTTGA\n+\nIIII\n' > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/at_quality.fastq
grep -c '^@' ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/at_quality.fastq
awk 'NR % 4 == 1' ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/at_quality.fastq | wc -l
pixi run seqkit stats -T ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/at_quality.fastq
```

```{.console}
3
2
file	format	type	num_seqs	sum_len	min_len	avg_len	max_len
/home/you/bioinf-computing-ch06/at_quality.fastq	FASTQ	DNA	2	8	4	4.0	4
```

Two reads; `grep` says 3. Counting header lines by **position**
(`awk 'NR % 4 == 1'`) gets 2, but only because the file has four lines
per read, and it checks nothing else. seqkit reads the format and gets 2
with no assumption. That is the same lesson as @sec-orientation: true for
this file is not true for FASTQ.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: `grep -c '^@'` is not a read count
`@` is also a quality character, so a quality line can start with it.
Count by position in a file you know has four lines per read, or, in
general, with `pixi run seqkit stats`.
:::

### Flags you will use

To see a whole read around a match, `-A 3` prints 3 lines **after** each
matching line:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | grep -A 3 '^@SRR6357070\.6710070 '
```

```{.console}
@SRR6357070.6710070 6710070/1 kraken:taxid|4932
GTCAGATTGGAAGTCATGGTCAGATTCTATGTTAAGATCATCGGATTGTTGGATCTCATTTGACGCAATGAACGATTGATATGAAGCAGTTAAACGGTTTA
+
BBBBBFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFB
```

The backslash before the dot and the space at the end make the pattern
exact; the next section explains both. When nothing matches, `grep`
prints nothing (or `0` with `-c`) and returns exit status `1`:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | grep -c ZZZZ
echo $?
```

```{.console}
0
1
```

Status 1 means "no match", not "error" (an error is 2). That matters in
scripts that stop on any nonzero status (@sec-shell-scripts).

: `grep` flags, with output on the book's files. {#tbl-grep-flags}

| Flag | Meaning | Example | Output here |
|:-----|:--------|:--------|:------------|
| `-c` | count matching lines | `grep -c '^@SRR'` (R1) | `50000` |
| `-v` | lines that do **not** match | `grep -v control samples.tsv` | the header and the two `treated` rows |
| `-i` | ignore case | `grep -i -c rep1 samplesheet_upstream.csv` | `4` |
| `-w` | whole words only | `grep -w treated samples.tsv` | the `sample_C` and `sample_E` rows |
| `-n` | show line numbers | `grep -n sample_B samples.tsv` | `4:sample_B…`, `6:sample_B…` |
| `-o` | print only the matching part | `grep -o 'SRR[0-9]*_1'` | one run name per line |
| `-A`, `-B`, `-C` | lines after, before, around a match | `grep -A 3 '^@SRR6357070\.6710070 '` | the whole read |
| `-F` | fixed string: no special characters | `grep -F -c 'fastq.gz'` | `7` |
| `-E` | extended regular expressions | `grep -E 'SRR[0-9]+'` | (@sec-text-tools-regex) |
| `-f file` | patterns from a file, one per line | `grep -f ids.txt` | for ID lists later |
| `-r` | search all files in a folder | `grep -r "seqkit" src/` | |

`zgrep` searches a `.gz` file directly: `zgrep -c '^@SRR'
data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz` also gives 50,000.

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** `gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | grep -c
CTG` gives 35,761. Is that the number of reads containing `CTG`?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Here, yes, but only because this file's quality lines use none of the
letters `C`, `T`, `G`. In general, search the sequence lines only:
`awk 'NR % 4 == 2' | grep -c CTG`. Both give 35,761 on this file.
:::
:::

## Regular expressions {#sec-text-tools-regex}

Count an EcoRI restriction site, `GAATTC`, in R1, then the same pattern
with one letter replaced by a dot:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | grep -c GAATTC
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | grep -c 'GA.TTC'
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | grep -o 'GA.TTC' | sort | uniq -c
```

```{.console}
2818
11404
   2901 GAATTC
   2917 GACTTC
   2483 GAGTTC
      1 GANTTC
   4083 GATTTC
```

Four times as many lines. In a `grep` pattern, `.` matches **any one
character**, and `grep -o` shows what it matched: `A`, `C`, `G`, `T`, and
once an `N`. (`-o` counts matches, so its numbers add up to more than the
2,818 matching lines.) The pattern is a **regular expression**, or regex:
a small language for describing text.

Two more on the sample sheet. List the run IDs, then count the FASTQ
file names:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
grep -o 'SRR[0-9]*_1' data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv | sed 's/_1$//'
grep -Eo 'SRR[0-9]+_[12]\.fastq\.gz' data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv | wc -l
```

```{.console}
SRR6357070
SRR6357071
SRR6357072
SRR6357073
SRR6357074
SRR6357075
SRR6357076
11
```

Seven runs, and 11 file names: four runs with two files each, plus
three runs that this test sheet uses as single-end, with one.
(`sed 's/_1$//'` removes the `_1` at the end; @sec-text-tools-sed-awk.) @fig-regex-anatomy takes the second
pattern apart.

::: {#fig-regex-anatomy}
{{< svg ../figures/regex-anatomy.svg >}}

The parts of `SRR[0-9]+_[12]\.fastq\.gz`, and three strings tested
against it. Only the first matches: `3` is not in `[12]`, and `\.` needs
a real dot.
:::

**Now name the parts.** Most characters match themselves (**literals**).
A few have special meanings (@tbl-regex-basics):

- `.` matches any one character; `\.` matches a real dot. The backslash
  turns a special character back into a literal.
- `[0-9]` matches one character from a **class**, here any digit;
  `[12]` matches `1` or `2`; `[^ACGT]` matches any character **except**
  those listed.
- `*` means "zero or more of the item before it", `+` "one or more",
  `?` "zero or one", and `{10,}` "10 or more".
- `^` and `$` anchor the match to the start and end of the line.
- `( )` groups, and `|` means "or": `^(WT|RAP1_IAA)` matches lines that
  start with either.

**Basic and extended syntax.** `grep` and `sed` use **basic** regular
expressions by default, where `+`, `?`, `{ }`, `( )`, and `|` are
ordinary characters unless you put a backslash before them. `grep -E`,
`sed -E`, and `awk` use **extended** syntax, where they are special
without one. So the same pattern behaves differently:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
grep -c 'SRR[0-9]+_' data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv
grep -Ec 'SRR[0-9]+_' data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv
```

```{.console}
0
7
```

In basic syntax, `+` was a literal plus sign, and no line contains one.
This book uses `-E` whenever a pattern needs `+`, `?`, `|`, or groups.
(GNU `grep -P` adds Perl-style patterns; you will meet it in other
people's commands.) Always put a regex in **single quotes**, so bash does
not treat `*`, `?`, `[ ]`, or `$` as its own special characters first.

: Regular expression basics. {#tbl-regex-basics}

| Piece | Meaning | Basic (`grep`, `sed`) | Extended (`grep -E`, `sed -E`, `awk`, R, Python) | Example |
|:------|:--------|:-------------------|:-------------------|:--------|
| `a` | the character itself | `a` | `a` | `GAATTC` |
| `.` | any one character | `.` | `.` | `GA.TTC` |
| `[ ]`, `[^ ]` | one character from, or not from, a set | `[12]`, `[^ACGT]` | same | `_[12]\.` |
| `*` | zero or more of the previous item | `*` | `*` | `SRR[0-9]*` |
| `+` | one or more | `\+` (GNU) | `+` | `SRR[0-9]+` |
| `?` | zero or one | `\?` (GNU) | `?` | `fastq(\.gz)?` |
| `{n,m}` | between n and m | `\{n,m\}` | `{n,m}` | `A{10,}` |
| `^`, `$` | start, end of line | `^`, `$` | same | `^@SRR`, `reverse$` |
| `\` | makes a special character literal | `\.` | `\.` | `\.fastq\.gz` |
| `( )`, `\|` | group, or | `\( \)`, `\|` (GNU) | `( )`, `\|` | `^(WT\|RAP1_IAA)` |

### Try patterns

@fig-regex-tester runs a pattern against eight fixed lines from the
book's files. Pick one of the examples from the list, or type your own.
Change one character at a time and watch what matches: try `GAATTC`,
then `GA.TTC`; `fastq.gz`, then `fastq\.gz`; `reverse$`, then
`reverse`.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof pattern = Inputs.text({
  label: "Pattern",
  value: "GA.TTC",
  placeholder: "type a regular expression",
  datalist: [
    "GAATTC", "GA.TTC", "^@SRR", "SRR[0-9]+_2\\.fastq\\.gz",
    "reverse$", "^(WT|RAP1_IAA)", "fastq.gz", "^[ACGT]+$"
  ],
  spellcheck: false
})
```

::: {#fig-regex-tester}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
testerLines = [
  "sample,fastq_1,fastq_2,strandedness",
  "WT_REP1,SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz,SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz,auto",
  "RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP1,SRR6357073_1.fastq.gz,,reverse",
  "RAP1_IAA_30M_REP1,SRR6357076_1.fastq.gz,SRR6357076_2.fastq.gz,reverse",
  "@SRR6357070.25017281 25017281/1 kraken:taxid|4932",
  "GTCAGACAACAACTTTTGGACCTTTGGAATTCTGGTAGAACC",
  "+",
  "BBBBBFFFFFFFBFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFB"
]

testerResult = {
  if (pattern === "") return {error: "Type a pattern.", rows: []};
  let re;
  try { re = new RegExp(pattern, "g"); }
  catch (e) { return {error: "Not a valid pattern: " + e.message, rows: []}; }
  const rows = testerLines.map((line) => {
    const parts = [];
    let last = 0, any = false;
    for (const m of line.matchAll(re)) {
      any = true;
      if (m[0].length === 0) continue;
      parts.push({text: line.slice(last, m.index), hit: false});
      parts.push({text: m[0], hit: true});
      last = m.index + m[0].length;
    }
    parts.push({text: line.slice(last), hit: false});
    return {line, parts, any};
  });
  return {error: null, rows};
}

{
  const lh = 22, top = 30, h = top + testerLines.length * lh + 30;
  const n = testerResult.rows.filter((r) => r.any).length;
  return htl.svg`<svg class="diagram" viewBox="0 0 720 ${h}" role="img"
      aria-label="${testerResult.error ?? `${n} of 8 lines match the pattern ${pattern}`}">
    <text x="8" y="18" font-size="13" class="fill-muted">${
      testerResult.error ?? `${n} of 8 lines match`}</text>
    ${testerResult.rows.map((r, i) => htl.svg`<g>
      <text x="8" y=${top + 14 + i * lh} font-size="13"
            class=${r.any ? "fill-given" : "fill-muted"}>${r.any ? "match" : "—"}</text>
      <text x="64" y=${top + 14 + i * lh} font-size="12.5" class="mono">${
        r.parts.map((p) => p.hit
          ? htl.svg`<tspan class="fill-given" font-weight="700" text-decoration="underline">${p.text}</tspan>`
          : htl.svg`<tspan class=${r.any ? "" : "fill-muted"}>${p.text}</tspan>`)
      }</text>
    </g>`)}
  </svg>`;
}
```

A regex tester on eight fixed lines from the sample sheet (shortened to
file names) and one FASTQ read. Lines that match say *match*; the
matched parts are underlined. It uses **JavaScript** regular
expressions, which agree with `grep -E` on the example patterns but not
in every detail.
:::

If the figure does not load, @tbl-regex-tester gives the same lesson:
what each example pattern matches in those eight lines, checked with
GNU `grep -E`.

: What the example patterns match in the tester's eight lines (1–4
sample-sheet lines, 5–8 a FASTQ read). {#tbl-regex-tester}

| Pattern | Lines that match | Why |
|:--------|:-----------------|:----|
| `GAATTC` | 6 | the exact site, in the sequence line |
| `GA.TTC` | 6 | `.` is any character; only one such place here |
| `^@SRR` | 5 | `@SRR` at the start: the header line |
| `SRR[0-9]+_2\.fastq\.gz` | 2, 4 | the R2 file names: rows with two files only |
| `reverse$` | 3, 4 | lines **ending** in `reverse` |
| `^(WT\|RAP1_IAA)` | 2, 4 | lines starting with either name |
| `fastq.gz` | 2, 3, 4 | would also match `fastqXgz`; `fastq\.gz` would not |
| `^[ACGT]+$` | 6 | the whole line is bases only |

Engines differ in details. GNU `grep -Eo 'a|ab'` on the text `ab` prints
`ab` (the longest match), while JavaScript's `/a|ab/` picks `a` (the
first alternative that fits). The tester's examples avoid such cases.

### Globs are not regular expressions

@sec-shell-basics promised this. A wildcard (glob) and a regex can look
alike and mean different things:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
grep -c '*.fastq.gz' data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv
grep -c '.*\.fastq\.gz' data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv
grep -o '[^/]*\.fastq\.gz' data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv | head -n 3
```

```{.console}
0
7
SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
SRR6357071_1.fastq.gz
```

`*.fastq.gz` as a **glob** means "any name ending in `.fastq.gz`". As a
regex it means something else: a `*` at the very start has nothing
before it to repeat, so `grep` reads it as a literal `*`, then any
character, then `fastq`, any character, `gz`. No line contains a `*`, so
0. In a regex, "anything" is `.*` and a real dot is `\.`: `.*\.fastq\.gz`
matches the 7 data rows. The third line prints the file names
themselves: `[^/]*` is "any run of characters that are not `/`", so the
match starts after the last `/` of each URL. (In a regex, "ends in
`.fastq.gz`" would be `\.fastq\.gz$`; no line of this sheet ends that
way, because each row ends with its strandedness.)

: The same characters in a glob and in a regex. {#tbl-glob-vs-regex}

| Characters | In a glob (`ls`, `find -name`) | In a regex (`grep`, `sed`, `awk`, R, Python) | Example |
|:-----------|:-------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------|:--------|
| `*` | any characters, including none | zero or more of the **previous** item | glob `*.gz`; regex `.*\.gz` |
| `?` | exactly one character | zero or one of the previous item (`-E`) | glob `run?`; regex `run.` |
| `.` | a literal dot | any one character | glob `*.fastq.gz`; regex `\.fastq\.gz$` |
| `[12]` | one of the characters | one of the characters | same in both |
| `[!1]` vs `[^1]` | `[!1]` not `1` | `[^1]` not `1` | |
| `^`, `$` | (no meaning) | start, end of line | regex `^SRR` |
| `{A,B}` | brace expansion: makes words | `{n,m}` repeats (`-E`) | glob `{R1,R2}`; regex `A{10,}` |

::: {.callout-caution .misconception}
## Misconception: "`*` means the same in `grep` as in `ls`"
**Reality.** In a glob, `*` is "any characters". In a regex, `*` is
"zero or more of the previous character", and `.` is "any character".
The regex for "anything" is `.*`.
:::

**The same regexes in R and Python.** Simple patterns like
`^SRR[0-9]+` work the same in R, `grepl("^SRR[0-9]+", x)` (base R uses
extended syntax), and in Python, `re.search(r"^SRR[0-9]+", s)`. But they
are separate engines, not one universal regex: base R, R's stringr
package, Python's `re`, JavaScript, and GNU `grep` differ in details such
as backslashes (R needs `"\\."` inside a string; Python's raw strings
`r"\."` avoid that) and which alternative wins in `a|ab`.
@sec-r-essentials and @sec-python-essentials use them. One warning for
all languages: regexes for structured formats, such as quoted CSV fields
or GTF attributes, get fragile fast; use a parser for those.

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** Does `grep 'fastq.gz'` match the text `fastqXgz`?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Yes: `.` matches any character, including `X`. Use `'fastq\.gz'`, or
`grep -F 'fastq.gz'`, which treats the whole pattern as plain text.
:::
:::

## Editing streams with `sed`, computing with `awk` {#sec-text-tools-sed-awk}

### `sed`: substitute

Chromosome names differ between sources: `chr1` in one, `1` in another
(@sec-fasta-fastq). Make a two-line toy file in the BED format and strip
the `chr`:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
printf 'chr1\t100\t200\nchr2\t300\t400\n' > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.bed
sed 's/^chr//' ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.bed
cat ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.bed
```

```{.console}
1	100	200
2	300	400
chr1	100	200
chr2	300	400
```

`sed` (stream editor) reads lines and writes them out, changed.
`s/^chr//` is a **substitution**: `s/pattern/replacement/`, here "replace
`chr` at the start of the line with nothing". The file itself is
unchanged, as `cat` shows: `sed` wrote the result to stdout, so save it
with `>` to a **new** file. Each `s` changes the first match on a line;
add `g` to change all of them:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
echo 'a-b-c' | sed 's/-/_/'
echo 'a-b-c' | sed 's/-/_/g'
```

```{.console}
a_b-c
a_b_c
```

The pattern is a basic regular expression, as in `grep`. When the
pattern contains `/`, pick another delimiter. File names from the URLs in
the sample sheet:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
tail -n +2 data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv | cut -d, -f2 | sed 's|.*/||'
```

```{.console}
SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
SRR6357071_1.fastq.gz
SRR6357072_1.fastq.gz
SRR6357073_1.fastq.gz
SRR6357074_1.fastq.gz
SRR6357075_1.fastq.gz
SRR6357076_1.fastq.gz
```

`s|.*/||` replaces "anything up to the last `/`" with nothing. (`.*`
matches as much as it can.) `sed` can do much more, but substitution is
what you need from it at this stage.

**`sed -i` edits a file in place.** It writes the changed text back into
the file. Two rules: never on `data/raw/`, and always run the command
**without** `-i` first and check the output. On a Mac, `sed -i` behaves
differently in the system's BSD `sed` (@sec-linux-system); this book uses
GNU `sed`.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Optional: FASTQ to FASTA with `sed`, and why to use seqkit instead

FASTA keeps only a header (starting with `>`) and the sequence. In a file
with exactly four lines per read, GNU `sed` can convert:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | head -n 8 | sed -n '1~4s/^@/>/p;2~4p'
```

```{.console}
>SRR6357070.25017281 25017281/1 kraken:taxid|4932
CCTGAATCGAGAAGGAGGTGTCCAGGGAGTTCATCATCAGAATGATTAGTATGATTTACTGTAGATTCAGTAAGTTTCTGGCCTAAGATGAAGGTCGTGCT
>SRR6357070.6710070 6710070/1 kraken:taxid|4932
GTCAGATTGGAAGTCATGGTCAGATTCTATGTTAAGATCATCGGATTGTTGGATCTCATTTGACGCAATGAACGATTGATATGAAGCAGTTAAACGGTTTA
```

`-n` prints nothing unless told to; `1~4` means "line 1, then every 4th
line" (GNU only), where `@` becomes `>` and the line is printed; `2~4p`
prints the sequence lines. It works only because of the four-line
layout. The format-aware command gives the same result with no such
assumption:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
pixi run seqkit head -n 2 data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | pixi run seqkit fq2fa
```

Use `seqkit fq2fa` on real files.
:::

### `awk`: fields and computing

Start with a mistake. Print column 3 of the practice table:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
awk '{print $3}' ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv
awk -F'\t' '{print $3}' ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv
```

```{.console}
condition
3
control
control
treated
control
control
condition
treated
control
control
treated
control
control
```

The first version printed `3` for `sample_C`, instead of `treated`. By
default `awk` splits each line into fields at **any** run of spaces or
tabs, so the run folder `Run 3 final` became three fields. `-F'\t'`
tells `awk` to split at tabs only. For tab-separated files, always use
it.

`awk` reads its input one line (a **record**) at a time and splits it
into **fields**, `$1`, `$2`, …; `$0` is the whole line. A program is a
list of `pattern {action}` pairs: for each line where the pattern is
true, run the action. Either part may be missing: `awk 'NR % 4 == 2'`
from @sec-text-tools-pipes has a pattern and no action, which means
"print the line". Add up the `reads` column:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 {s += $4} END {print s}' ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv
tail -n +2 ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv | sort -u | awk -F'\t' '{s += $4} END {print s}'
```

```{.console}
194
164
```

`NR > 1` skips the header (`NR` is the record number); `s += $4` adds
field 4 to a running total `s`, which starts at 0; `END { … }` runs once,
after the last line. 194 with the duplicated `sample_B` row, 164 without
it, as promised in @sec-text-tools-counting.

A filter with a condition, and output with tabs:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 && $4 > 20' ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv
awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' 'NR > 1 {print $1, $4}' ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv
```

```{.console}
sample_B	run2	control	30
sample_E	run5	treated	105
sample_B	run2	control	30
sample_C	12
sample_A	9
sample_B	30
sample_E	105
sample_B	30
sample_D	8
```

`&&` means "and". In `print $1, $4`, the comma puts the **output field
separator** between fields, a space by default; `-v OFS='\t'` makes it a
tab, so the output is tab-separated too.

**Fields in the annotation.** A GTF line has nine tab-separated fields,
and the ninth, the attributes, contains spaces (@fig-awk-fields). That is
another reason for `-F'\t'`.

::: {#fig-awk-fields}
{{< svg ../figures/awk-fields.svg >}}

A GTF line (the CDC19 transcript) split by `awk -F'\t'` into nine
fields, `$1` to `$9`, with the column names below. Field 9 contains
spaces, so `awk`'s default splitting would break it apart.
:::

Count transcripts per strand: column 3 is the feature and column 7 the
strand.

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c data/ref/genes.gtf.gz | awk -F'\t' '$3 == "transcript"' | cut -f7 | sort | uniq -c
```

```{.console}
     60 -
     64 +
```

124 transcript lines: 64 on the plus strand and 60 on the minus strand.
In this file each transcript has one line, and each gene one
transcript, but that is a property of this file, not of GTF. `==`
compares; text values go in double quotes.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Optional: the longest transcript spans

For readers who want to see `awk` compute a column: the span of each
transcript on the genome is `end − start + 1`. The `match()` part pulls
the gene ID out of field 9; take it as given (GTF attributes are
@sec-intervals-variants).

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c data/ref/genes.gtf.gz \
  | awk -F'\t' '$3 == "transcript" {match($9, /gene_id "[^"]+"/); print $5 - $4 + 1, substr($9, RSTART + 9, RLENGTH - 10)}' \
  | sort -k1,1nr | head -n 3
```

```{.console}
4614 YAR050W
4416 YAL029C
4308 YAL024C
```

A span on the genome is not the length of the spliced transcript;
coordinates are @sec-intervals-variants.
:::

**Check one tool against another.** Add up the `num_seqs` column of the
seqkit table you saved with `tee`:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 {s += $4} END {print s}' ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts.tsv
```

```{.console}
100000
```

100,000 reads in two files, and remembering @sec-getting-help's meaning
check: two mate files, so **50,000 read pairs**. Now count the `N`
bases (unknown bases) in each file with `awk`:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2 {n += gsub(/N/, "")} END {print n}'
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2 {n += gsub(/N/, "")} END {print n}'
```

```{.console}
280
18842
```

`gsub(/N/, "")` removes every `N` from the line and returns how many it
removed, and `n` adds them up. 280 and 18,842: exactly seqkit's `sum_n`
column from @sec-getting-help's Exercise 2. (Every `N` also has the
quality character `#`, the lowest score in this file, and no other base
does: one more independent count that agrees.) Two independent
tools agree, so you can trust the one-liner.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Check a one-liner against something independent
Before trusting a new one-liner, compare it with a count you got
another way: here `awk`'s `N` count and seqkit's `sum_n`.
:::

: The parts of `awk` used in this chapter. {#tbl-awk-basics}

| Piece | Meaning | Example |
|:------|:--------|:--------|
| `$1`, `$2`, … | fields of the current line | `{print $3}` |
| `$0` | the whole line | `{print length($0)}` |
| `NF` | number of fields on the line | `{print NF}` |
| `NR` | record (line) number | `NR > 1`, `NR % 4 == 2` |
| `-F'\t'` | split fields at tabs only | `awk -F'\t' …` |
| `pattern {action}` | run the action on lines where the pattern is true | `$3 == "transcript" {print $7}` |
| pattern alone | print matching lines | `awk '$4 > 20'` |
| `BEGIN {…}`, `END {…}` | run before the first line, after the last | `END {print s}` |
| `-v OFS='\t'` | separator between printed fields | `print $1, $4` |
| `gsub(/re/, "x")` | replace all matches; returns the count | `n += gsub(/N/, "")` |

When a one-liner grows past one line, it belongs in a script
(@sec-shell-scripts), or in R or Python (@sec-r-essentials,
@sec-python-essentials), where it can be read, tested, and reused.

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** What does
`gunzip -c data/ref/genes.gtf.gz | awk -F'\t' '$7 == "-"' | wc -l`
count?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Lines on the minus strand, of **every** feature type (transcripts,
exons, CDS, codons): 296 here. Not genes.
:::
:::

## Compressed files {#sec-text-tools-compression}

You have read `.gz` files through `gunzip -c` all chapter. `gzip` writes
them too, and as a filter it compresses whatever arrives on stdin. Save
the first 100 reads of R1 as a small compressed file, then check it:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | head -n 400 | gzip > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/small_R1.fastq.gz
gunzip -c ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/small_R1.fastq.gz | wc -l
gzip -t ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/small_R1.fastq.gz
```

```{.console}
400
```

400 lines, and `gzip -t` is silent: intact. 400 lines are 100 reads
**only** in a file with four lines per read; the general recipe is
`pixi run seqkit head -n 100`, as in @sec-getting-help.

Compress a stream you made yourself, the 50,000 sequence lines:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2' | gzip -c > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/seqs.txt.gz
ls -l ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/seqs.txt.gz
```

```{.console}
-rw-r--r-- 1 you you 853893 Nov 17 20:49 /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch06/seqs.txt.gz
```

About 850 KB for 5.1 MB of text (the exact size depends on the gzip
version). DNA compresses well because it uses only a few letters.

**The family.** `gzip file` compresses `file` into `file.gz` and removes
the original; `gunzip file.gz` does the reverse. `-c` writes to stdout
instead and leaves the input alone, which is what you want almost
always. `zcat file.gz` is the same as `gunzip -c file.gz` in GNU gzip,
and you will see it in other people's scripts. This book writes
`gunzip -c` because the `zcat` built into macOS does not read `.gz`
files:

```{.console}
zcat: can't stat: data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz (data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz.Z): No such file or directory
```

(It looks for a `.Z` file, an older format.) On Linux, `zcat` works the
same as `gunzip -c`.

**Rules for big files.**

- Do not decompress a large file to disk to read it: stream it with
  `gunzip -c … |`. A 10 GB `.fastq.gz` is 40 GB or more uncompressed.
- Many tools read `.gz` directly, including seqkit and most aligners, so
  a decompressed copy is rarely needed.
- Reading a 10 GB file through a pipe is real work: on a cluster, do it
  in a job, not on the login node (@sec-hpc-slurm).
- `bgzip` is a variant of gzip that allows jumping to a position inside
  the file; indexed genomics files use it (@sec-intervals-variants).
  `pigz` is a parallel gzip that uses several cores (@sec-performance).

: Working with gzip files. {#tbl-compression}

| Task | Command | Note |
|:-----|:--------|:-----|
| check a file is intact | `gzip -t f.gz` | silent when intact (@sec-orientation) |
| read | `gunzip -c f.gz \| head` | `zcat` on Linux; not macOS's `zcat` |
| browse | `zless f.gz` | @sec-shell-basics |
| search | `zgrep -c pattern f.gz` | same flags as `grep` |
| write compressed | `cmd \| gzip > out.gz` | never over the input |
| compress, keep original | `gzip -k f` | without `-k`, `f` is removed |
| indexable compression | `bgzip f` | for indexed genomics files (@sec-intervals-variants) |
| faster on many cores | `pigz` | @sec-performance |

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: decompressing to disk
`gunzip big.fastq.gz` writes the full uncompressed file and deletes the
`.gz`. Stream instead with `gunzip -c big.fastq.gz | …`, or give the
`.gz` file to a tool that reads it directly.
:::

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** Why stream a 10 GB `.fastq.gz` with `gunzip -c … |`
instead of running `gunzip file.fastq.gz` first?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
No 40 GB or larger uncompressed copy on disk or in your quota, and the
file is read once instead of twice.
:::
:::

## Text tools and format-aware tools {#sec-text-tools-format-aware}

You did several jobs in this chapter with text tools. Each has a tool
that understands the file format (@tbl-text-vs-format).

: Text tools and format-aware tools for the jobs in this chapter.
{#tbl-text-vs-format}

| Task | Text-tool way | Format-aware tool | Where the text tool breaks |
|:-----|:--------------|:------------------|:---------------------------|
| count reads | `wc -l` ÷ 4, `awk 'NR % 4 == 1'` | `seqkit stats` | records not exactly four lines |
| count reads by header | `grep -c '^@'` | `seqkit stats` | quality lines that start with `@` |
| FASTQ to FASTA | `sed -n '1~4s/^@/>/p;2~4p'` | `seqkit fq2fa` | multi-line records |
| first N reads | `head -n 400` | `seqkit head -n 100` | multi-line records |
| reads with a motif | `awk` + `grep -c` | `seqkit grep -s` | both strands, mismatches |
| filter a GTF by feature | `awk -F'\t' '$3 == "exon"'` | an annotation package (@sec-intervals-variants) | attribute parsing, comment lines |
| count alignments | (not text: BAM is binary) | `samtools view -c` (@sec-sam-bam-cram) | compressed binary format |

The format-aware tool wins once files are real: records that span
several lines (every `NR % 4`, `head -n 400`, and `1~4` in this chapter
assumed four lines per read), comment and header lines, quoted fields,
binary formats such as BAM, variants of compression, and the `@` trap.
Text tools stay the best way to **look** at a file and to check a result
quickly: count lines, find the odd one, compare two columns. Part IV
opens with the same principle.

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
Use text tools to look and to check; use format-aware tools to process.
:::

## Summary {#sec-text-tools-summary}

- A pipe `|` joins one program's stdout to the next one's stdin, with no
  file in between. Build pipelines one step at a time and look at each
  step's output.
- `>` replaces a file and `>>` appends; the shell empties a `>` target
  **before** the command runs, so never redirect onto your input: write
  a new file, check it, `mv` it. `tee` saves and shows at once.
- Results go to stdout and messages to stderr, by convention. `2>`,
  `2>&1`, and `/dev/null` route stderr on purpose; a pipeline's status is
  its last command's, so read the messages and check counts against what
  you expect.
- `cut`, `sort`, `uniq -c`, and `wc` count and summarise columns; sort
  before `uniq`, use `sort -n` for numbers and `LC_ALL=C` for a
  reproducible order. `grep` finds lines and `-c` counts them.
- A regular expression describes text (`.`, `[ ]`, `*`, `+`, `^`, `$`,
  `\`); it is not a glob. `sed 's/…/…/'` substitutes; `awk -F'\t'`
  selects fields and computes. Stream `.gz` files with `gunzip -c`, and
  use format-aware tools to process real FASTQ, BAM, and annotation.

: The chapter's commands on one page. {#tbl-ch06-commands}

| Task | Command |
|:-----|:--------|
| Pipe, save, append, show and save | `cmd1 \| cmd2`, `> f`, `>> f`, `\| tee f` |
| Errors to a file, both to a log, discard | `2> err.txt`, `> log 2>&1`, `2> /dev/null` |
| Count lines, see invisible characters | `wc -l`, `cat -A` |
| Columns, count values | `cut -f3`, `cut -d, -f1`, `sort \| uniq -c` |
| Sort | `sort -n`, `sort -t$'\t' -k4,4n`, `sort -k1,1nr`, `LC_ALL=C sort` |
| Skip a header | `tail -n +2` |
| Find lines | `grep -c`, `-v`, `-w`, `-o`, `-A 3`, `-E`, `-F` |
| Substitute | `sed 's/^chr//'`, `sed 's|.*/||'` |
| Fields and sums | `awk -F'\t' '$3 == "x" {print $7}'`, `awk 'NR > 1 {s += $4} END {print s}'` |
| Compressed files | `gunzip -c`, `\| gzip >`, `gzip -t`, `zgrep`, `zless` |
| Compare two files | `cmp a b` (Exercise 3) |

## Exercises {#sec-text-tools-exercises}

Run every exercise from `~/bioinf-computing`, and write outputs to
`~/bioinf-computing-ch06`.

::: {.check}
**Exercise 1. Build a pipeline step by step.** Start from
`gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz | head -n 8` and add one step
at a time, checking the output after each, until the pipeline reports
how many reads of each length R2 has. Then remove the `head`. Record the
final command and its result in `NOTEBOOK.md`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz | head -n 8 | awk 'NR % 4 == 2'
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz | head -n 8 | awk 'NR % 4 == 2 {print length($0)}'
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2 {print length($0)}' | sort | uniq -c
```

```{.console}
  50000 101
```

The same as R1: all 50,000 reads are 101 bases. Keeping `head` while you
build makes each check instant.
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 2. Fix the redirections.** First make a copy of the seqkit
table to work on:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cp ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts.tsv ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts_copy.tsv
```

Each of the four lines below has a redirection problem. Say what goes wrong,
then write a fixed version. Run them only after you have predicted the
result.

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cut -f1,4 ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts_copy.tsv
pixi run seqkit stats -T ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/broken.fastq.gz > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/stats.tsv 2>&1
sort -t$'\t' -k4,4n ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts_copy.tsv > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts_copy.tsv
```

The third line empties the copy, so make it again before the fourth,
and run the fourth line **twice**:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cp ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts.tsv ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts_copy.tsv
cut -f1 ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts_copy.tsv >> ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/files.txt
```

The goal: the per-file read counts saved in a file, seqkit's table in
`stats.tsv` and its messages in a log, the sorted table in its own file
with the input untouched, and `files.txt` holding each file name once
however often you run the line.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer

1. The counts only go to the screen. Fix: add
   `> ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/reads_per_file.tsv`.
2. `2>&1` puts the `[ERRO]` lines, with their colour codes, into the
   results file, ahead of the header. Fix: `> …/stats.tsv 2> …/stats.log`.
3. The input is emptied before `sort` reads it (`wc -c` shows 0 bytes).
   Fix: `> ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts_sorted.tsv`, check it, and only
   then `mv` if you want to replace the original.
4. `>>` adds the names again on every run, so after two runs each name is
   there twice. Fix: `>`.

Start the fixed versions from a fresh copy, since line 3 emptied it:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cp ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts.tsv ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts_copy.tsv
cut -f1,4 ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts_copy.tsv > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/reads_per_file.tsv
pixi run seqkit stats -T ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/broken.fastq.gz > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/stats.tsv 2> ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/stats.log
sort -t$'\t' -k4,4n ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts_copy.tsv > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts_sorted.tsv
cut -f1 ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts_copy.tsv > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/files.txt
```

The fixed `stats.tsv` holds only the header, because the file is broken;
the reason is in `stats.log`.
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 3. Do the mates match?** Aligners pair reads by position: read
1 in R1 with read 1 in R2, and so on (@sec-fasta-fastq). Check that the
two files list the same reads in the same order. In this file a header
looks like `@SRR6357070.25017281 25017281/1 kraken:taxid|4932` (R2:
`…/2 …`): the mate number sits inside the second field, and the **first
field** is the same in both mates. Write that field for every record,
count the lines, and compare the files with `cmp`, which prints nothing
when two files are identical:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz \
  | awk 'NR % 4 == 1 {print $1}' > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R1.txt
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz \
  | awk 'NR % 4 == 1 {print $1}' > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R2.txt
wc -l ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R1.txt ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R2.txt
head -n 3 ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R1.txt
cmp ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R1.txt ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R2.txt
echo $?
```

Then make a copy of `ids_R2.txt` with line 3 changed, and compare again:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
sed '3s/$/x/' ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R2.txt > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R2_bad.txt
cmp ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R1.txt ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R2_bad.txt
echo $?
```

Why are both the line count and `cmp` needed?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer

```{.console}
  50000 /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R1.txt
  50000 /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R2.txt
 100000 total
@SRR6357070.25017281
@SRR6357070.6710070
@SRR6357070.5843839
0
```

```{.console}
/home/you/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R1.txt /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R2_bad.txt differ: char 61, line 3
1
```

50,000 IDs in each file, identical and in the same order: `cmp` is
silent and its status is `0`. The altered copy differs at line 3
(`sed '3s/$/x/'` added an `x` to the end of line 3), status `1`. `cmp`
is also silent for two **empty** files, so the line count proves the
extraction worked. This is a check for this four-line file; @sec-fasta-fastq
does it with format-aware tools.
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 4. Summarise the annotation.** Using `cut`, `sort`,
`uniq -c`, and `awk -F'\t'` on `data/ref/genes.gtf.gz`, and
@fig-awk-fields for the column numbers, find: the feature types and
their counts; the sequence names and their counts; and the transcript
lines per strand. Which line is on a sequence that is not in the
genome? Note your commands and answers in `NOTEBOOK.md`.

**Extension (optional).** GTF attributes are @sec-intervals-variants, so
these two commands are supplied. Run them and say what each counts:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c data/ref/genes.gtf.gz | grep -o 'gene_id "[^"]*"' | sort -u | wc -l
gunzip -c data/ref/genes.gtf.gz | awk -F'\t' '$3 == "transcript"' \
  | grep -o 'gene_biotype "[^"]*"' | sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Feature types: the chapter's pipeline, `cut -f3 | sort | uniq -c |
sort -k1,1nr`: 129 exon, 124 transcript, 118 CDS, 115 start_codon,
114 stop_codon. Sequence names, `cut -f1 | sort | uniq -c`: 599 `I`,
1 `not_in_genome`. Strands, `awk -F'\t' '$3 == "transcript"' | cut -f7 |
sort | uniq -c`: 60 `-`, 64 `+`. The odd line is line 1 (`grep -n
not_in_genome` prints `1:`), a CDS on `not_in_genome`.

Extension: 124 distinct gene IDs; and the gene types of the transcripts:

```{.console}
124
    116 gene_biotype "protein_coding"
      4 gene_biotype "tRNA"
      2 gene_biotype "pseudogene"
      1 gene_biotype "ncRNA"
      1 gene_biotype "snoRNA"
```
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 5. Regex practice on the sample sheet.** Write one `grep -E`
that matches only the R2 file names in
`data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv`, and count them. Then write one
`awk -F,` command that prints the sample labels of the rows given as
single-end, those with an empty `fastq_2` (column 3).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
grep -Eo 'SRR[0-9]+_2\.fastq\.gz' data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv | wc -l
awk -F, '$3 == "" {print $1}' data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv
```

```{.console}
4
RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP1
RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP2
RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP2
```

Four R2 files, one per row with two files. `RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP2`
appears twice because the test sheet puts that label on two rows used as
single-end; in the archive they are two different paired-end samples
(@sec-organizing-projects-metadata). Without `-o`, `grep -c`
would count lines, which is also 4 here.
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 6. Check with a second tool.** Count the R1 reads that
contain the exact motif `AGATCGGAAGAGC`, first with `grep -c` on the
sequence lines (as in @sec-text-tools-grep), then with seqkit:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
pixi run seqkit grep -s -P -C -p AGATCGGAAGAGC data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
```

`-s` searches the sequences, `-P` the given (positive) strand only, `-p`
gives the pattern, and `-C` counts the matching reads (seqkit's `-C`, not
`grep`'s `-c`). Do the numbers agree? Then make a one-read file that holds
only the **reverse complement** of the motif, and run both tools on it,
and seqkit once more without `-P`:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
printf '@rc\nGCTCTTCCGATCT\n+\nIIIIIIIIIIIII\n' > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/revcomp.fastq
awk 'NR % 4 == 2' ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/revcomp.fastq | grep -c AGATCGGAAGAGC
pixi run seqkit grep -s -P -C -p AGATCGGAAGAGC ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/revcomp.fastq
pixi run seqkit grep -s -C -p AGATCGGAAGAGC ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/revcomp.fastq
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
On R1 both give 1,916. On the toy file, `grep` gives 0 and seqkit with
`-P` gives 0, but seqkit without `-P` gives 1: by default `seqkit grep
-s` searches **both** strands, and the reverse complement of the motif is
the motif read from the other strand. On the real files both settings
give 1,916 (R1) and 1,910 (R2), so only the toy file shows the
difference. A second tool is a real check only when you know what each
one counts.
:::
:::

## Further reading {#sec-text-tools-reading}

- @shotts2025linux, *The Linux Command Line*, chapters on redirection,
  regular expressions, and text processing --- the same tools with more
  examples, at a gentler pace; free online.
- @wilson2019swcarpentry, Software Carpentry's [*The Unix
  Shell*](https://swcarpentry.github.io/shell-novice/), episodes "Pipes
  and Filters" and "Finding Things" --- a second walk-through with
  exercises, written for researchers.
- @buffalo2015bioinformatics, *Bioinformatics Data Skills*, its chapter
  on Unix data tools --- the closest match to this chapter in audience
  and examples: genomic text files, `sort -k`, `join`, and `awk` on
  annotation.
- @gnu2025grep, the [GNU Grep
  manual](https://www.gnu.org/software/grep/manual/), section *Regular
  Expressions* --- short and exact on basic vs extended syntax. The
  [GNU coreutils](https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/),
  [sed](https://www.gnu.org/software/sed/manual/), and
  [gawk](https://www.gnu.org/software/gawk/manual/) manuals cover the
  other tools, and [POSIX's
  chapter](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/basedefs/V1_chap09.html)
  defines regular expressions formally.
- @aho2023awk, *The AWK Programming Language*, 2nd edition --- by awk's
  authors, for readers who want much more `awk`; optional.
